This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The Director (PI) is managing the final stages of an EMNLP 2026 ARR paper submission (DDL: 2026-05-25) for the "gen-depth-fingerprint" project. The core research is about Differential Depth Response (DDR) in recursive LLM generation chains. Key user requests during this session:
   - Process W1 completion (cross-model LOGO evaluation update from sample-level CV to generator-level LOGO)
   - Fix all numerical inconsistencies found by Reviewer across paper/supplement
   - User explicitly requested: "现在在跑实验吗，刚才说对提分有帮助的实验都跑完了吗，要充分利用已有的gpu，尽量不要浪费" (use GPUs, don't waste them)
   - User requested: "大胆尝试所有可能调至3.5的改善方法" (try all improvements to raise score from 3.0 to 3.5)
   - Run experiments to strengthen paper before DDL
   - Write experiment results into paper appendices

\subsection{9-Generator Scale Evaluation}\label{app:9gen-scale}

This analysis extends the 8-generator LOGO evaluation to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).
All results use class-balanced LOGO; the 8-gen averages here (0.770/0.701) differ slightly from Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} (0.762/0.694), which uses an unfiltered protocol.
Table~\ref{tab:9gen-logo} reports per-generator LOGO performance under this expanded set.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llr cc cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 1.0B & 0.857 & [0.848, 0.866] & 0.785 & --- \\
Qwen3-0.6B      & Qwen    & 0.6B & 0.819 & [0.807, 0.830] & 0.743 & --- \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & Qwen    & 1.7B & 0.811 & [0.800, 0.823] & 0.746 & --- \\
OLMo-2-1B       & OLMo    & 1.5B & 0.773 & [0.762, 0.784] & 0.692 & --- \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3.2B & 0.759 & [0.748, 0.770] & 0.680 & --- \\
Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 8.2B & 0.696 & [0.683, 0.709] & 0.647 & [0.631, 0.664] \\
Gemma-2-2B      & Gemma   & 2.6B & 0.628 & [0.622, 0.634] & 0.440 & [0.432, 0.449] \\
Mistral-7B      & Mistral & 7.0B & 0.605 & [0.593, 0.617] & 0.534 & --- \\
\midrule
\textbf{Average (9-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.751} & & \textbf{0.666} & \\
\textbf{Average (8-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.770} & & \textbf{0.701} & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Overall comparison.}
Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
The per-generator F1 values for the original eight generators shift by at most $[-0.011, +0.002]$, indicating that the inclusion of Gemma data in training does not destabilize existing generalization patterns.

\paragraph{Gemma-2-2B anomaly.}
Gemma-2-2B is the weakest held-out generator: 3-class F1\,=\,0.628, binary F1\,=\,0.440.
Per-class breakdown reveals a striking asymmetry: gen-0 F1\,=\,0.991 and gen-2+ F1\,=\,0.856, but gen-1 F1\,=\,0.036---the classifier almost entirely fails to identify first-generation Gemma continuations.
This is not a data-quality artifact: the Gemma-2-2B partition contains 4{,}957 instances with a balanced depth distribution ($\sim$990 per level).
A plausible explanation is that Gemma-2's first-generation continuations occupy a region of feature space highly similar to human-written text (gen-0), causing systematic misclassification of gen-1 as gen-0 or gen-2+.
This constitutes an architecture-specific generalization limitation rather than a systemic failure of the depth fingerprinting approach.

\paragraph{Scale effect.}
A clear parameter-count gradient emerges across the nine generators: three of four sub-1.7B generators achieve F1\,$>$\,0.81 (OLMo-2-1B at 0.773 is the exception), mid-range models (2--3B) cluster at 0.63--0.81, and large models (7B+) fall to 0.60--0.70.
Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters) achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.696 under the 9-gen split, compared to 0.701 in the class-balanced 8-gen evaluation; this small difference reflects the changed training composition rather than a property of the Qwen3-8B generator itself.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses confirm that DDR features carry causal predictive power beyond correlation: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, and 6/7 features exhibit significant Granger causality across generation depths, with entropy\_min as the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow 1.0$: overall 3-class F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.723; the most affected single generator, Qwen3-1.7B, drops to per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
This divergence has practical implications: model collapse remediation focuses on restoring tail coverage, while inference-chain contamination preserves shape and thus requires location-based detection---a strategy that DDR directly enables.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), but QLoRA on instruct data (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91 vs.\ XGBoost 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal, though this is demonstrated under within-model CV only; cross-generator instruct transfer (XGBoost LOGO F1\,=\,0.487) remains weak.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Gemma-2-2B shows the weakest generalization among nine generators (3-class F1\,=\,0.628), with gen-1 nearly indistinguishable from other classes (per-class F1\,=\,0.036); this architecture-specific limitation is discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}.
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

This appendix validates the causal predictive power of DDR features through three complementary analyses: permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention.

\paragraph{Permutation Importance.}
Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance} reports the mean F1 drop when each feature's values are randomly shuffled across the test set (baseline F1\,=\,0.771).
Drifting features dominate: their average F1 drop (0.187) is $5.5\times$ larger than the near-stationary average (0.034), confirming that location-shift features---not shape features---drive depth classification.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcr}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Group} & \textbf{Mean F1 Drop} & \textbf{Rank} \\
\midrule
hapax\_ratio  & Drifting      & 0.235 & 1 \\
entropy\_mean & Drifting      & 0.170 & 2 \\
ttr           & Drifting      & 0.156 & 3 \\
entropy\_max  & Near-stat.    & 0.070 & 4 \\
entropy\_std  & Intermediate  & 0.057 & 5 \\
entropy\_min  & Near-stat.    & 0.019 & 6 \\
tail\_decay   & Near-stat.    & 0.014 & 7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Permutation importance (8-gen LOGO). Each feature is shuffled independently; the resulting F1 drop quantifies marginal importance. Drifting features average $0.187$ vs.\ near-stationary $0.034$ ($5.5\times$).}
\label{tab:perm-importance}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger Causality.}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} reports Fisher-combined $p$-values from panel Granger causality tests (lag\,=\,1) across 8 generators ($N$\,=\,29{,}095).
Six of seven features exhibit significant Granger causality ($p < 0.001$), meaning past feature values predict future depth beyond what past depth alone explains.
The sole exception is entropy\_min ($p$\,=\,0.375), providing additional evidence for its near-stationary classification: it carries neither large marginal importance (Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance}, rank 7) nor temporal predictive direction.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Combined $p$} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta R^2}$ & \textbf{Significant} \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & $< 0.001$ & 0.031 & Yes \\
hapax\_ratio  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
ttr           & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_mean & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_max  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
tail\_decay   & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_min  & $0.375$   & ---   & No  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Granger causality (Fisher combined across 8 generators, lag\,=\,1, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). $\Delta R^2$ is reported where available.}
\label{tab:granger}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Key Findings.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Drifting dominance.} The $5.5\times$ permutation-importance gap confirms that drifting features (entropy\_mean, ttr, hapax\_ratio) are the primary depth signal carriers, consistent with the DDR partition derived from convergence analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

\item \textbf{Entropy\_min lacks causal direction.} Beyond its small effect size (F1 drop\,=\,0.019), entropy\_min is the only feature without significant Granger causality ($p$\,=\,0.375). This strengthens the near-stationary classification: the feature is neither marginally important nor temporally predictive.

\item \textbf{Entropy\_max asymmetry.} Entropy\_max ranks fourth in permutation importance (F1 drop\,=\,0.070) but produces the largest degradation in the counterfactual intervention ($-$2.0\,pp), indicating that it provides unique signal not redundant with other features---its causal contribution exceeds its marginal importance.

\item \textbf{Mistral heterogeneity.} In per-generator Granger tests, Mistral-7B shows non-significant hapax\_ratio and ttr ($p > 0.4$), though Fisher combination across generators remains significant. This generator-specific attenuation partly explains Mistral's lowest LOGO F1 (0.605) and suggests that DDR fingerprints are weaker in models with heavier repetition penalties.
\end{enumerate}

This is consistent with recursive generation inducing a **location shift** in the NLL distribution while approximately preserving distributional shape. The contribution is: (a) the **task formulation** (generation depth classification beyond binary detection), (b) **empirical validation** across 8 generators / 5 model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B–8B) showing DDR is robust, (c) a lightweight 7-feature ensemble achieving leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores show moderate signal but high cross-generator variance.

**Our framing**: We formulate generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) and characterize DDR across 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B). Central-tendency features drift monotonically while shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO with a single 410M reference model. Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 at 2.4× cost. The signal degrades under instruction tuning and high temperature, restricting current scope to base models at moderate temperatures.

**Headline result template**: "On 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B), our 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under LOGO evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M reference model. Depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (TOST p = 1.1×10⁻⁴ at ±2% margin), establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

**RC1 — "Is this just vocabulary impoverishment?"**: Surface features alone achieve 0.688, but full features achieve 0.773 (McNemar p ≈ 0). Reference features capture different, complementary signal. Reference-only yields higher binary F1 (0.833) but misses gen-0 discrimination. The complementarity itself is a finding.

**RC2 — "Does this generalize beyond Pythia?"**: 8 generators from 5 families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral). LOFO binary F1 = 0.686 confirms cross-family transfer. Cross-model chains (heterogeneous generators per depth step) yield binary F1 = 0.764.

**RC3 — "Is 3-class sufficient?"**: 5-class F1 drops to ~0.50. Ordinal methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement. Gen-1/gen-2+ boundary is the resolution bottleneck. 3 classes represent practical ceiling.

**RC4 — "How realistic are single-model chains?"**: Cross-model chains (different generator per step) are evaluated and yield higher F1 (0.764 binary), suggesting generator heterogeneity amplifies distributional shifts.

**RC5 — "What about human editing?"**: Robustness test with simulated human edits (random word replacement + LLM-simulated editing). Reported in appendix.

**RC6 — "Ecological validity?"**: Multi-domain seeds (news, Wikipedia, scientific, creative) + multiple prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting). Prompt-type dependence reported transparently (continuation 0.781 vs elaboration 0.730).

**RC8 — "Aren't these just OOD detection features?"**: Contribution is NOT the features but: (a) ordinal depth estimation formulation, (b) empirical DDR discovery (drifting vs stationary), (c) Findings-level empirical characterization. Paper explicitly connects to OOD/perplexity-based detection literature.

**RC9 — "Only base models — what about instruct?"**: Acknowledged as primary limitation. OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs 0.763 base. Instruction tuning compresses the distributional variation DDR exploits. Reported transparently; defines scope boundary.

**RC10 — "Text length confound"**: Length-matched subsampling: binary F1 = 0.724 (vs 0.770 unmatched). Random-subsample control confirms drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction.

**RC11 — "Downstream — limited evidence"**: Three seeds, single perplexity metric. TOST equivalence confirmed at ±2% margin for equal-count comparison. Margin sensitivity analysis across ±1%–5% reported. Cohen's d inflated by low seed-level variance; TOST is the appropriate test.

## Contribution Positioning (Findings Level)
The contribution is **empirical and conceptual**, appropriate for Findings:
1. **Problem formulation**: Generation depth classification as a new task beyond binary detection (no prior work addresses this in non-paraphrastic chains)
2. **Empirical characterization**: DDR across 8 generators / 5 families (0.6B–8B), with cross-generator generalization (LOGO binary F1 = 0.694, LOFO 0.686, cross-model 0.764). Honest reporting of scope boundaries (instruct degradation, temperature sensitivity, scale effect).
3. **Negative finding**: Depth-aware curation ≡ random subsampling for downstream quality (TOST confirmed). Depth fingerprinting is diagnostic, not curative.

**Framing discipline:**
- Do NOT call the drift/stationarity split a "discovery" — it follows from location-shift properties of the NLL distribution. Acknowledge explicitly.
- Do NOT use H1/H2 terminology. Use "drifting" vs "stationary" or "differential response."
- Do NOT overclaim "dual dynamics." Use "differential depth response" (DDR).
- Report **realistic performance range** (binary F1 0.633–0.724 per-generator, 0.694 LOGO average) in abstract/conclusion, not best-case.
- Primary metric is leak-free binary F1 (not 3-class, which is inflated by gen-0 seed sharing).
- 7-feature ensemble is positioned on efficiency, not absolute superiority over multi-detector ensembles.

Related work must cover: perplexity-based detection (DetectGPT, GLTR, DNA-GPT, Binoculars), model collapse theory, OOD detection, data quality scoring, watermarking, vocabulary diversity, stylometry/authorship attribution, iterative generation (LLM as Broken Telephone ACL 2025), membership inference.

## Venue Fit
- EMNLP 2026 Findings: Excellent fit — directly addresses data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, data governance. Empirical/conceptual contribution with honest scope boundaries. Findings-appropriate ambition level: novel task formulation + solid characterization, not a state-of-the-art methodology claim.

\subsection*{Instruction-Tuned Model Results}

Table~\ref{tab:instruct} summarizes depth classification under instruction tuning for three model families.
All results use within-model 5-fold CV on single-generator chains; LOGO evaluation is available for two models but uses earlier generator subsets (5--6 generators), so cross-model numbers are not directly comparable across rows.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Depth classification: base vs.\ instruction-tuned models (within-model 5-fold CV). $\rho$: Spearman correlation of entropy mean with depth. Rev.: number of features (out of 7) whose $\rho$ reverses sign under instruction tuning.}
\label{tab:instruct}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcc cc cc c}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{3-class F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Binary F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\boldsymbol{\rho}$\textbf{(ent.\ mean)}} & \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \cmidrule(lr){4-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-7}
\textbf{Model} & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & \textbf{Rev.} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B       & 0.754 & 0.575 & 0.845 & 0.813 & $-$0.64 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & 0.769 & 0.732 & 0.861 & 0.875 & $-$0.60 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & 0.742 & 0.544 & 0.849 & 0.838 & $-$0.63 & $+$0.23 & 3/7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Instruction tuning degrades 3-class F1 by 3.7--19.9\,pp across all three families, while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) changes remain small ($|\Delta| \leq 3.2$\,pp).
The asymmetry indicates that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary (human vs.\ first-generation), consistent with RLHF shifting the output distribution away from human-like text.
Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign for all three models ($-0.60$--$-0.64$ base $\rightarrow$ $+0.23$--$+0.48$ instruct), and 6 of 7 features reverse for OLMo and Qwen vs.\ 3 of 7 for Llama.
This pattern is consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than eliminating iterative dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Retraining on instruction-tuned data.}
To test whether the depth signal persists under instruction tuning with reversed polarity, we retrain the XGBoost classifier on instruction-tuned feature data (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-retrain}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Classification recovery under instruction-tuned retraining (binary-only: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, gen-0 excluded from training and evaluation). Base$\rightarrow$Inst: base-trained classifier tested on instruct data. Note: Table~\ref{tab:instruct} reports higher instruct binary F1 (e.g., OLMo 0.813) because it uses 3-class training with binary evaluation, where gen-0 in training helps the classifier learn the feature space.}
\label{tab:instruct-retrain}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Base$\rightarrow$Inst} & \textbf{Retrained} & \textbf{$\Delta$} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B-Inst   & 0.321 & 0.590 & $+$0.269 \\
Qwen3-1.7B-Inst  & 0.500 & 0.660 & $+$0.160 \\
Qwen3-0.6B-Inst  & 0.532 & 0.600 & $+$0.068 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Retraining recovers substantial within-model performance ($+$6.8--26.9\,pp), but the retrained F1 (0.590--0.660) remains below base-model levels (0.69--0.72).
Three-generator instruct LOGO yields binary F1\,=\,0.487, indicating weak cross-generator transfer under instruction tuning.

\paragraph{DDR structure under instruction tuning.}
$k{=}2$ clustering in $(|\rho|, d)$ space on pooled instruct features yields silhouette\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.632 for base models), indicating that the clean drifting/non-drifting partition is substantially compressed.
The compression is model-dependent: OLMo-Instruct shows near-zero $|\rho|$ for TTR and hapax (0.006, 0.025), while Qwen instruct models retain moderate correlations ($|\rho|{=}0.48$--$0.53$).
Cross-condition transfer is near chance in both directions (base$\rightarrow$instruct binary F1\,=\,0.490; instruct$\rightarrow$base F1\,=\,0.454), with the asymmetry ($-$0.036) suggesting that instruct-trained features generalize even less to base distributions than the reverse.
These results indicate that instruction tuning compresses the feature-space structure underlying DDR rather than simply reversing feature directions.

\paragraph{End-to-end instruct classification.}
To test whether depth signal persists at the token level despite summary-statistic degradation, we apply the QLoRA end-to-end classifier (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) to instruction-tuned data using within-model 5-fold stratified CV (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-qlora}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{End-to-end QLoRA vs.\ XGBoost on instruction-tuned data (within-model 5-fold CV, Qwen3-0.6B backbone). Base QLoRA rows shown for reference only; instruct sets ($N{\approx}4.4$--$5.0$K) are approximately twice the base sets ($N{\approx}2.3$K), so cross-condition comparison is confounded by training set size.}
\label{tab:instruct-qlora}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{3-class F1}} & & \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3}
\textbf{Model} & XGB & QLoRA & $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ & \textbf{$N$} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B-Inst   & 0.575 & 0.888\,$\pm$\,0.007 & $+$31.3\,pp & 4{,}429 \\
Qwen3-1.7B-Inst  & 0.732 & 0.907\,$\pm$\,0.008 & $+$17.5\,pp & 4{,}963 \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B (base) &       & 0.859\,$\pm$\,0.004 &             & 2{,}379 \\
Qwen3-1.7B (base)&       & 0.904\,$\pm$\,0.009 &             & 2{,}291 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The XGBoost-to-QLoRA gap on the same instruct data is substantial ($+$17.5 to $+$31.3\,pp), indicating that depth signal persists at the token level under instruction tuning but is inaccessible to the seven summary statistics; the degradation reported in Table~\ref{tab:instruct} reflects a feature-level limitation rather than signal absence.
Note that instruct samples are approximately twice the base count used here (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-qlora}), so the instruct-vs-base QLoRA comparison is confounded by training set size; the meaningful comparison is QLoRA-vs-XGBoost on the same instruct data.
All results use within-model 5-fold CV, not cross-generator LOGO, limiting generalization claims.

0	# Paper Framing — gen-depth-fingerprint
1	
2	## Target Venue
3	- **Primary: EMNLP 2026 Findings (ARR deadline: May 25, 2026)** — D012: 恢复为主投稿目标
4	- Positioning: **Findings paper**（非 main conference long paper）
5	- Fallback venues: ICLR 2027 (Sep 24), NAACL 2027 ARR (Oct 16)
6	
7	## Core Insight
8	Non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains exhibit **differential depth response** (DDR): **central-tendency/diversity features** (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with depth, while **shape features** (entropy_max, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. This is consistent with recursive generation inducing a **location shift** in the NLL distribution while approximately preserving distributional shape. The contribution is: (a) the **task formulation** (generation depth classification beyond binary detection), (b) **empirical validation** across 8 generators / 5 model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B–8B) showing DDR is robust, (c) a lightweight 7-feature ensemble achieving leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO. Depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current scope to base models.
9	
10	## Core Claims (3 条，均可证伪)
11	
12	**Claim 1 — Depth Discriminability**: A 7-feature distributional ensemble can classify generation depth (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen-2+) with leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 (95% CI [0.688, 0.700]) under 8-generator LOGO evaluation, generalizing across unseen generators and model families (LOFO binary F1 = 0.686). Cross-model chains yield binary F1 = 0.764. Primary metric is leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs gen-2+), excluding gen-0 to avoid seed-sharing leakage.
13	
14	**Claim 2 — Differential Depth Response & Feature Complementarity**: Features exhibit DDR: drifting features show |ρ| > 0.60 (hapax −0.63, TTR −0.61, entropy_mean −0.60), while shape features show |ρ| < 0.10 (tail_decay 0.04). KS statistics confirm: drifting 0.516–0.537 vs shape 0.043–0.052 (~10× gap). Full 7-feature set (10-fold CV F1 = 0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar p ≈ 0). Reference-only yields higher binary F1 (0.833 vs 0.695) but surface features are essential for 3-class gen-0 discrimination.
15	
16	**Claim 3 — Downstream Utility (Negative Finding)**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality. At equal sample count (n=3,951): random subsampling (ppl=2.367) outperforms depth 0–1 (2.387) and binary-filtered (2.389). TOST confirms equivalence at ±2% margin (p = 1.1×10⁻⁴). Full dataset (n=12,299, ppl=2.335) vs depth-filtered requires ±3% margin for equivalence. Depth fingerprinting is a **diagnostic** tool for provenance characterization, not a **curative** tool for data selection.
17	
18	## Headline Metrics Summary
19	
20	| Metric | Value | Context |
21	|--------|-------|---------|
22	| **Primary: LOGO binary F1** | **0.694** [0.688, 0.700] | 8-gen LOGO, gen-1 vs gen-2+, leak-free |
23	| LOGO 3-class F1 | 0.762 [0.758, 0.766] | Inflated by gen-0 seed sharing |
24	| Cross-model binary F1 | 0.764 | 5-gen subset, 5-fold CV |
25	| Cross-model 3-class F1 | 0.809 | 5-gen subset, 5-fold CV |
26	| LOFO binary F1 | 0.686 | Leave-one-family-out |
27	| Per-gen binary F1 range | 0.633–0.724 | Mistral-7B lowest, Pythia-2.8B highest |
28	| Feature ablation (10-fold CV) | Full 0.773, Surface 0.688, Ref 0.713 | McNemar p ≈ 0 |
29	| Length-matched binary F1 | 0.724 vs 0.770 unmatched | Deconfounding, not sample-size effect |
30	
31	## Scope & Limitations (必须在论文中突出)
32	
33	1. **Base models only**: Instruct-tuned models show substantially degraded signal (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs 0.763 base). Alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation DDR exploits. This is the **primary scope limitation**.
34	2. **Temperature sensitivity**: Reliable within t ∈ [0.5, 0.9] (≤1 pp degradation from default t=0.7). At t = 1.0: −6 pp degradation; entropy_mean ρ drops from −0.60 to −0.002. Cross-temperature transfer degrades severely (t=0.7 → t=1.0: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops 0.789 → 0.418).
35	3. **7-feature ensemble is not optimal**: Multi-detector ensembles (4-det + surface) achieve 3-class 0.795 vs 0.774 (+2.1 pp) and binary 0.708 vs 0.705 (+0.3 pp), but at 2.4× inference cost and 3.2× GPU memory. 7-feature positioned on **efficiency advantage**, not absolute performance.
36	4. **3-class resolution ceiling**: 5-class F1 drops to ~0.50; ordinal methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost. Gen-1/gen-2+ boundary is the bottleneck (concentrates 86% of binary errors as FNs).
37	5. **Scale effect**: Larger generators show moderate degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633, Qwen3-8B: 0.692 vs average 0.694). Higher-capacity models compress feature margins.
38	6. **Prompt-type dependence**: Continuation chains show stronger drift (F1 = 0.781) than elaboration (0.730).
39	
40	## Story Spine
41	
42	**Problem**: Web-scraped training data increasingly contains LLM-generated text of unknown provenance depth (7–17% of recent scientific papers). Current detection methods offer only binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material: gen-1 retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
43	
44	**Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score) cannot distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+. Attractor cycle theory (ACL 2025) bounds paraphrasing chains to ~3 classes but depends on semantic-preservation constraints. No existing method addresses generation depth estimation in non-paraphrastic continuation chains. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores show moderate signal but high cross-generator variance.
45	
46	**Our framing**: We formulate generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) and characterize DDR across 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B). Central-tendency features drift monotonically while shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO with a single 410M reference model. Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 at 2.4× cost. The signal degrades under instruction tuning and high temperature, restricting current scope to base models at moderate temperatures.
47	
48	**Headline result template**: "On 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B), our 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under LOGO evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M reference model. Depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (TOST p = 1.1×10⁻⁴ at ±2% margin), establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization."

## Scope & Limitations (必须在论文中突出)

1. **Base models only**: Instruct-tuned models show substantially degraded signal (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs 0.763 base). Alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation DDR exploits. This is the **primary scope limitation**.
2. **Temperature sensitivity**: Reliable within t ∈ [0.5, 0.9] (≤1 pp degradation from default t=0.7). At t = 1.0: −6 pp degradation; entropy_mean ρ drops from −0.60 to −0.002. Cross-temperature transfer degrades severely (t=0.7 → t=1.0: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops 0.789 → 0.418).
3. **7-feature ensemble is not optimal**: Multi-detector ensembles (4-det + surface) achieve 3-class 0.795 vs 0.774 (+2.1 pp) and binary 0.708 vs 0.705 (+0.3 pp), but at 2.4× inference cost and 3.2× GPU memory. 7-feature positioned on **efficiency advantage**, not absolute performance.
4. **3-class resolution ceiling**: 5-class F1 drops to ~0.50; ordinal methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost. Gen-1/gen-2+ boundary is the bottleneck (concentrates 86% of binary errors as FNs).
5. **Scale effect**: Larger generators show moderate degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633, Qwen3-8B: 0.692 vs average 0.694). Higher-capacity models compress feature margins.
6. **Prompt-type dependence**: Continuation chains show stronger drift (F1 = 0.781) than elaboration (0.730).

## Story Spine

**Problem**: Web-scraped training data increasingly contains LLM-generated text of unknown provenance depth (7–17% of recent scientific papers). Current detection methods offer only binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material: gen-1 retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score) cannot distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+. Attractor cycle theory (ACL 2025) bounds paraphrasing chains to ~3 classes but depends on semantic-preservation constraints. No existing method addresses generation depth estimation in non-paraphrastic continuation chains. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores show moderate signal but high cross-generator variance.

**Our framing**: We formulate generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) and characterize DDR across 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B). Central-tendency features drift monotonically while shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO with a single 410M reference model. Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 at 2.4× cost. The signal degrades under instruction tuning and high temperature, restricting current scope to base models at moderate temperatures.

**Headline result template**: "On 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B), our 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under LOGO evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M reference model. Depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (TOST p = 1.1×10⁻⁴ at ±2% margin), establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization."

Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.830 (95\% CI [.818, .841]) under generator-level leave-one-out evaluation on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available (Pythia-2.8B/1B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B).\footnote{We corrected the cross-model chain evaluation from sample-level CV to generator-level LOGO for consistency with our main evaluation protocol. CIs are case-level bootstrap ($n$\,=\,2{,}000). The 5-generator result is not directly comparable to the 8-generator LOGO (binary F1\,=\,0.694) due to differing generator subsets.}
The higher cross-model binary F1 relative to the 8-generator LOGO (0.694) is not directly comparable: the cross-model evaluation uses a 5-generator subset, and generator heterogeneity in mixed chains may amplify depth-correlated distributional shifts.
A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, consistent with cross-family transfer.
A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-generator LOGO; $+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), which indicates that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
